question: A non-precise cache-miss profile puts most samples on an `add` that uses the value of the preceding load. What is the most likely reading?
options: The add instruction is unusually slow on this CPU
The profile is broken and should be discarded
Cache misses are caused by arithmetic instructions
The load is the real culprit; skid moved the recorded IP to a later instruction
explain: Skid means the IP is captured some instructions after the event. The add depends on the load, so it is where the stall shows up. Re-record with :pp to have PEBS or IBS attribute the samples to the load itself.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: A latency-critical service shows p99 spikes on allocation-heavy requests and a fast-rising compact_stall. THP is enabled=always, defrag=always. Which change targets the spikes while keeping most THP benefit?
options: Set defrag to defer so faults fall back to small pages and khugepaged collapses later
Set max_ptes_none to 0
Raise khugepaged pages_to_scan
Switch enabled to madvise and defrag to always
explain: The spikes come from direct compaction inside page faults. defer stops faults from stalling and leaves the work to kcompactd and khugepaged. max_ptes_none and pages_to_scan only affect khugepaged, not fault stalls, and madvise mode with defrag=always still stalls in any region the app marks.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: The SSM layer inside a hybrid: Mamba-2 as gated linear attention
question: During decoding at 100K tokens of context, which part of a Mamba-2 layer's per-sequence memory grows with the context?
options: The SSM state h
The convolution buffer
Both, linearly in context length
Neither; both have fixed size
explain: Both the state (heads x head dim x N) and the convolution window (4 inputs) are fixed by the architecture. That fixed size is exactly why hybrids use these layers, and also why they cannot store unlimited exact detail.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion: fusing by rank, not score
question: With k = 60, BM25 returns documents scoring 41.2 and 40.9 at ranks 1 and 2, and a second run with a different tokenizer returns 9.3 and 2.1 at ranks 1 and 2. How do the RRF contributions of these four positions compare?
options: The first run contributes far more because its scores are larger
Rank 1 gets 1/61 and rank 2 gets 1/62 in both runs; raw score gaps are ignored
The second run contributes more because its gap between ranks is bigger
They cannot be compared without normalizing first
explain: RRF uses only positions. That makes it immune to score scales (good) but blind to the fact that the second run is much more confident about its top hit (information lost). Bruch et al. argue this loss of score information is one reason a tuned convex combination can beat RRF.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: The HyDE pipeline: generate, encode, average, search
question: Your corpus index was built with Contriever. A colleague proposes embedding the hypothetical documents with a different, stronger embedding model to save effort. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, any embedding model works with any index
Only latency increases
The LLM must then be retrained
The vector lands in a different embedding space, so inner products with the indexed Contriever vectors are meaningless
explain: HyDE relies on document-document similarity inside one space. The hypothetical passage must be encoded by the same encoder f that encoded the corpus, otherwise the averaged vector and the index vectors are not comparable.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
question: Why does a homography have 8 degrees of freedom rather than 9?
options: Because H and any nonzero multiple of H map every point to the same place
Because h9 is always 1 by definition
Because one equation per point is redundant
Because the bottom row must be (0, 0, 1)
explain: Scaling H scales X, Y and W together, and the division X/W, Y/W cancels it. So only 8 independent quantities matter. Setting h9 = 1 is a convention that fails when the true h9 is 0, and a fixed bottom row (0, 0, 1) would make H affine.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Cleaning the mask and correcting for lighting
question: Why does ECC alignment tolerate a change in exposure between the two images?
options: It compares zero-mean, normalized intensity vectors, so gain and offset cancel
It converts images to edges first
It uses RANSAC on pixel intensities
It only runs on binary masks
explain: The enhanced correlation coefficient subtracts each image's mean (removing an offset) and divides by its norm (removing a gain). Evangelidis and Psarakis point out that this makes the criterion invariant to brightness and contrast changes. It does not model local shadows.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Fixed resources, polling, multishot networking and tradeoffs
question: A configuration service does about 50 small reads per second in short bursts, on a 2-core VM that is already busy. A teammate proposes `IORING_SETUP_SQPOLL` to save system calls. Good idea?
options: Yes, SQPOLL always lowers latency
Yes, but only with IORING_SETUP_IOPOLL as well
No: at 50 I/O per second the syscalls saved are negligible, and the poll thread competes for one of only 2 busy CPUs and keeps going to sleep between bursts
No, because SQPOLL requires root on all kernels
explain: SQPOLL pays off when a stream of submissions keeps the thread busy. Here it would mostly spin or sleep and wake, costing CPU on a constrained machine for almost no saved work. Privilege is no longer required on recent kernels, so that is not the reason.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: Cross-thread frees, idle caches and returning memory
question: A latency-sensitive service shows p99 spikes every few seconds, and a profile shows time in page faults right after memory was purged. Which change targets this most directly?
options: Increase the number of size classes
Disable the thread cache
Lengthen the purge delay (jemalloc dirty_decay_ms or MIMALLOC_PURGE_DELAY) so freed pages stay mapped longer between bursts
Lower jemalloc's opt.narenas to 1
explain: The spikes come from returning pages to the OS and faulting them back in. A longer delay keeps them resident across bursts, at the cost of higher RSS. Disabling caches or arenas adds contention without fixing the faults.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: The nemesis: partitions, pauses, clocks and crashes
question: A coordination service hands out locks that expire if the holder misses heartbeats for 2 s. Which nemesis is most likely to show two clients holding the same lock?
options: Process pauses with SIGSTOP and SIGCONT lasting longer than the lease
A partition that isolates one follower that holds no locks
Bit flips in a log file on a single node
Packet duplication on a client link
explain: A paused holder cannot notice its lease expiring, so another client acquires the lock, and the first resumes believing it still holds it. Isolating an uninvolved follower or flipping bits does not target the lease mechanism.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Prune before you measure: shared memory and registers
question: A config that uses 144 KiB of shared memory tunes fine on a cc 9.0 GPU. The same tuning job runs on a cc 8.6 GPU and that config is now rejected. What should the tuner do?
options: Reduce num_stages automatically until it fits and keep the measured timing
Treat the limit as device state: prune against this device's limit and re-tune, because the legal space itself changed
Keep the cc 9.0 result, since the config is still correct code
Fail the tuning run, because the config list is invalid
explain: Shared memory per block is a documented per-capability quantity (227 KB at 9.0, 99 KB at 8.6), so the set of legal configurations is part of the device, not the kernel. Silently rewriting num_stages produces a config nobody measured, and carrying the old winner over is exactly the stale-cache failure of the next lesson.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
question: Why do DPDK and SPDK allocate I/O buffers from hugepages rather than plain malloc memory?
options: Because NICs cannot DMA into 4 KiB pages
Because VFIO only accepts 1 GiB pages
Because hugepages are faster for the device to read over PCIe
Because hugepages have physical addresses that Linux does not move today and are contiguous within a page, and they also cut TLB misses
explain: The device must be given addresses that stay valid. Hugepages are not migrated by Linux today and each one is physically contiguous; the TLB benefit is a bonus. With an IOMMU, VFIO pins and maps them explicitly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The price of bypass, and when to choose something else
question: A key-value service handles 50,000 requests per second per machine, shares cores with other services, and runs on laptops for development. Should it adopt DPDK?
options: Probably not: per-request kernel overhead is a tiny part of its budget, and bypass would burn dedicated cores, need root-level device setup and lose kernel tooling
Yes, bypass always lowers latency
Yes, but only with UIO to avoid needing an IOMMU
Yes, because hugepages alone will double its throughput
explain: At 50k requests per second each request has about 20 us of one core, so saving a microsecond of kernel path is noise. Bypass pays off near line rate, not for ordinary services.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: A fused kernel for a long row-wise reduction starts spilling registers and runs slower than two unfused kernels. Which fix matches what FlashAttention and Triton tutorials do?
options: Tile the reduction so each block of the row fits on chip, carrying running statistics between tiles
Fuse even more ops into the kernel
Switch to FP64 to get more registers
Disable the GPU's L2 cache
explain: Fusion is bounded by on-chip capacity. Tiling with running statistics (as in FlashAttention's online softmax) keeps the working set small while still avoiding HBM round trips for intermediates.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Distilling language models: tokens, sequences, on-policy
question: You can call a strong model only through a text API that returns completions, not probabilities. Which method can you still use?
options: Word-level distillation with soft targets
Sequence-level distillation: train the student with cross-entropy on the teacher's generated outputs
On-policy GKD with forward KL
Logit matching at high temperature
explain: Seq-KD only needs the teacher's output sequences. Word-level KD, logit matching and GKD all need the teacher's token-level probabilities (white-box access) on the relevant prefixes.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
question: A colleague quantizes both keys and values per-token at 2 bits and sees accuracy collapse, while 4-bit per-token worked fine. What is the most likely fix?
options: Use 3-bit per-token for both
Quantize values per-channel and keep keys per-token
Quantize keys per-channel and keep values per-token
Add more calibration data
explain: Per-token key groups get their range stretched by outlier channels, which wipes out the small channels at 2 bits. Per-channel keys fix that. In KIVI's Llama-2-13B test, keys per-token with values per-channel scored 2.80 on CoQA, worse than all per-token.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Compressing long prompts (SnapKV, PyramidKV) and choosing a recipe
question: Using the bars, which move gives the larger capacity gain over GQA-8 BF16: FP8, or keeping 20% of tokens in BF16?
options: FP8, about 2x
They are equal
20% kept, about 5x
Neither changes capacity
explain: FP8 halves bytes per token (59 to 119 sequences). Keeping 20% of tokens cuts per-sequence cache 5x (59 to 297), but with the risk of losing information permanently.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Eviction and placement: what stays, what sinks, what is dropped
question: A chatbot has 1,000 active sessions that each return every 5 minutes, and the host tier holds 600 sessions. Under strict LRU, what hit rate should you expect for returning sessions, and why?
options: About 60%, because the tier holds 60% of sessions
100%, because LRU keeps recently active sessions
About 50%, because LRU and FIFO behave the same here
Close to 0%, because each session is the least recently used by the time it returns, so it was just evicted
explain: With a cyclic access pattern larger than the cache, LRU evicts the oldest session, which is exactly the next one to return. Every return misses. Admission filtering that keeps a fixed subset resident, a bigger tier (SSD) or scheduler look-ahead all fix this; matching capacity alone does not.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Hybrid logical clocks: Lamport order that stays near real time
question: A node is at (10, 3). It performs a local event when its physical clock reads 11. What timestamp does the event get?
explain: l = max(10, 11) = 11, which differs from the old l, so c resets to 0: (11, 0). The reset is what keeps c bounded: as soon as the physical clock catches up with l, all accumulated ties are forgotten.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Inside the encoders: markers, [MASK] padding and training
question: A user types the 3-word query *who founded pixar*. With the default query length of 32, how many query vectors take part in MaxSim?
options: 3, one per word
4, one per WordPiece token
7, the tokens plus [CLS], [Q] and [SEP]
32, because the query is padded with [MASK] to 32 positions and every position yields a vector
explain: ColBERT pads every query to N_q = 32 with [MASK] tokens, and every position's output vector is used in MaxSim. So the query matrix is always 32 x 128, and the mask vectors act as learned expansion terms.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
question: In one step of ordinary CoT decoding, which operation discards the most information about the model's internal state?
options: The attention layers, because they average over earlier positions
Sampling a single token from softmax(W h), since only its identity is passed on
The final layer normalization before the LM head
The positional encoding added to the next input
explain: The next pass sees only e(x) for the one sampled token, a vector chosen from a fixed table of 50,257 rows. Everything else in the 768-dimensional h(t), including how probable the alternatives were, is dropped. Attention and normalization transform information but pass a full vector on.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs
question: Adding 6 pause tokens vs. adding 6 Coconut thoughts to a 12-layer model: what happens to the longest serial chain of layer computations before the answer?
options: Both grow to 84 layers
Pause: stays 12. Coconut: grows to about 84
Pause: grows to 84. Coconut: stays 12
Both stay at 12 because attention is parallel
explain: A pause slot's input is a fixed embedding, so its computation happens in the same pass and every path climbs at most 12 layers. Each Coconut thought is the top-layer output of the previous pass fed in at the bottom, so 6 thoughts plus the final pass give 7 x 12 = 84.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: PGM-index: guaranteed error with optimal linear segments
question: Why can uniform random keys need about as many segments as log-normal keys at epsilon 8?
options: The greedy algorithm is not optimal for uniform data
Uniform keys have duplicates
Linear models cannot represent a uniform CDF
At small scale, random gaps make the positions deviate from any line by more than 8 slots, so the distribution's global shape barely matters
explain: The uniform CDF is a straight line globally, but the actual positions of random keys wander around that line, and over 400,000 keys those excursions exceed 8 slots often. With a larger epsilon the wiggles fit inside the band and uniform data collapses to a single segment at eps 512. Model the data you have, not the distribution it came from.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Scoring as a sparse dot product over an inverted index
question: In doc-only mode, what work remains at query time?
options: Tokenizing the query and traversing the inverted index
Running the full transformer on the query
Re-encoding every candidate document
Nothing; results are precomputed per query
explain: The query is tokenized with the same vocabulary and each token gets a fixed weight (1 in SPLADE-doc, or a lookup table in OpenSearch). No transformer runs at query time.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: RankNet: a probability for every pair
question: Two documents with different labels currently have identical scores. What is the RankNet cost of that pair (sigma = 1)?
options: 0, because the scores are not in the wrong order
ln 2, about 0.693, so the pair is still pushed apart
Infinite, because the probability is undefined
1, the maximum of the sigmoid
explain: At s_i = s_j the sigmoid gives P = 0.5 and C = ln(1 + e^0) = ln 2. Burges calls this a built-in margin: equal scores for differently labeled documents are still penalized.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
question: Why does regrouping $(QK^\top)V$ as $Q(K^\top V)$ fail for softmax attention?
options: Matrix multiplication is not associative
The softmax is applied to each row of $QK^\top$ before multiplying by V, so the product cannot be regrouped
Softmax attention uses different key and query dimensions
The causal mask makes regrouping impossible for any attention
explain: Associativity only holds for plain products. Softmax applies a nonlinear exp and normalization to every entry of $QK^\top$ first. Causal masking alone is fine: the running sum $S_t$ handles it.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Chunkwise training and hybrid models in production
question: Qwen3-Next's context grows from 32K to 256K tokens. Which part of its per-sequence cache grows?
options: Only the KV cache of the 12 full-attention layers; the Gated DeltaNet state stays 72 MiB
Only the Gated DeltaNet state
Both grow 8x
Neither grows
explain: Gated DeltaNet layers keep a fixed $d_k\times d_v$ state per head regardless of length. The attention layers' KV cache grows linearly: 768 MiB at 32K to 6,144 MiB at 256K, while the 72 MiB state is unchanged.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Judge biases: position, verbosity and self-preference
question: Your pairwise judge compares old ranker versus new ranker results and always shows the new ranker's result first. It reports a 58% win rate for the new ranker. What should you do first?
options: Ship the new ranker, 58% is a clear win
Rerun every comparison with the order swapped and count a win only when both orders agree; inconsistent pairs become ties
Switch to a longer prompt so the judge reads more carefully
Ask the judge to explain its reasoning and trust the explanation
explain: With a fixed order, position bias is confounded with the treatment. Swap-and-tie (Zheng et al.) removes the position effect: wins must survive both orders. Randomising the order per pair is the cheaper large-scale alternative.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: KV cache accounting: from bytes per token to batch size
question: Llama 3 70B has 80 layers, 64 query heads, 8 KV heads and head dimension 128. What is its BF16 KV cache per token?
options: 160 KiB
2.5 MiB
320 KiB
640 KiB
explain: 2 x 80 x 8 x 128 x 2 = 327,680 bytes = 320 KiB. Using the 64 query heads instead of the 8 KV heads gives 2.5 MiB (the GQA mistake); dropping the factor 2 for K and V gives 160 KiB; using 4-byte values gives 640 KiB.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a prompt: rules, delimited inputs and the task
question: You need answers about a 40,000-token contract. Following Anthropic's long-context advice, where should the question go?
options: At the very top, so the model knows what to look for before reading
Inside the contract tags, next to the relevant clause
After the contract, at the end of the prompt
In a separate request, without the contract
explain: Anthropic recommends long documents near the top and the query at the end, reporting up to 30 percent better responses in its tests. Putting the question inside the data tags blurs data and instructions; a separate request loses the document.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: From regex to JSON Schema: grammars, stacks and real engines
question: Why can no regular expression enforce arbitrarily nested JSON, while a fixed shape like {"ok": boolean} is fine?
options: Matching brackets at any depth needs unbounded memory, and an FSM has only finitely many states
Regular expressions cannot match quote characters
JSON is not text, so regex engines cannot read it
Regexes are too slow for long outputs
explain: An FSM's only memory is its current state. To close n open brackets correctly it would need distinct states for every n, which no finite machine has. A fixed shape has bounded depth, so it compiles to a finite machine; general JSON needs a grammar with a stack.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Evaluating the parser with exact match per field
question: A parser gets each of 7 fields right 90 percent of the time, independently. Roughly what whole-object exact match should you expect?
options: 90 percent, the same as each field
about 63 percent
about 48 percent
about 10 percent
explain: Exact match needs all 7 right: 0.9 to the power 7 is about 0.478. This is why object exact match looks harsh and why per-field scores are needed to see what to fix. Real field errors are correlated (a confusing query breaks several), which usually makes EM a bit better than the independent estimate.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Latency: the dependency chain decides, not the call count
question: A team measures 10 s per query for RankGPT-style listwise reranking of the top 100 on a self-hosted 7B model. They double GPU count. What do you expect for a single query in isolation?
options: About 5 s, since work is split in half
About 20 s, from coordination overhead
About the same 10 s, since the 9 windows are a dependent chain
About 1 s, since all windows now run at once
explain: Each window reads the list as reordered by the previous window, so the windows cannot overlap within one query. More GPUs help when many queries run concurrently.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Distilled 7B rerankers versus a cross-encoder: choosing a design
question: Our estimate says the 7B listwise pass uses about 1,000 times the forward FLOPs of the MiniLM cross-encoder on the same 100 candidates. What is a valid reason to still use the LLM?
options: It reads fewer tokens
On your measured queries it ranks the top results better, and a cascade can limit it to a short list
Its calls are independent
FLOPs do not affect GPU time
explain: The LLM is used for quality, not efficiency. A cascade confines the expensive model to the few candidates where order matters most.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Cost in LLM calls, tokens and latency
question: Your latency budget is tight but you can run many LLM calls in parallel. Which method has the fewest sequential rounds for 100 candidates?
options: PRP-Sliding-10
Listwise with w 20, s 10
Setwise bubble sort
PRP-Allpair
explain: All 9,900 Allpair calls are independent, so with enough parallel capacity they finish in one round, the same as pointwise. Sliding, listwise and setwise sorting are chains of dependent calls. Allpair is still the most expensive in total compute and tokens.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Matching descriptors and Lowe's ratio test
question: A brick wall has hundreds of nearly identical corners. Your matcher returns many matches with small d1 but ratio near 0.95. What should you conclude?
options: They are ambiguous: the repeated texture gives several near-equal neighbors, so most should be rejected
These are the most reliable matches because d1 is small
The ratio threshold should be raised to 1.0 for walls
Switch from L2 to Hamming distance to fix it
explain: A ratio near 1 means the second-best neighbor is almost as close as the best, so the descriptor cannot tell which brick is which. That is exactly the ambiguity the ratio test exists to remove. Changing the distance metric does not fix repetition.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Treiber stack: one CAS on the top pointer
question: A colleague changes push's successful CAS to `memory_order_relaxed` to "save a fence". What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, CAS is always sequentially consistent on every CPU
Two pushes can both succeed on the same top
A popping thread may see the new node pointer but stale or uninitialized value and next fields
Pop will spin forever
explain: Atomicity of the CAS is unaffected, so two pushes cannot both win. What is lost is ordering: without release (paired with pop's acquire), the plain stores to n->value and n->next are not guaranteed visible to the thread that pops n. Some CPUs happen to be strongly ordered, but the C++ model allows the bug and compilers may reorder too.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
question: You need a fixed-capacity MPMC queue between 16 producers and 16 consumers, and producers may be preempted. Which statement is accurate?
options: A Vyukov-style ring has one CAS per operation and no per-item allocation, but a producer preempted after claiming a slot can delay consumers behind it
A Vyukov-style ring is wait-free
Only a Michael-Scott queue can be bounded
A Treiber stack gives FIFO order if you pop twice
explain: That is the tradeoff from lesson 5 exactly: cheap and allocation-free, blocking in the corner case where a claimant stalls. If that corner case is unacceptable, use a truly lock-free design and pay for reclamation.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: From templates to counts, time series and alerts
question: You switch parsers and your DeepLog-style sequence model's false positive rate explodes overnight, even though the new parser scores higher group accuracy on the benchmark. What is the most likely cause?
options: The new parser is slower, so events arrive out of order
The new parser assigns different template ids, so the model's vocabulary no longer matches the stream and it sees unfamiliar keys
Group accuracy is irrelevant to sequence models
The LSTM needs retraining on every release regardless of the parser
explain: The model's vocabulary is the template set it was trained on. A different parser splits, merges and renumbers templates, so sequences that were normal now contain keys the model never saw. This is why template ids must be stable artifacts, and why a parser swap requires retraining every model downstream of it, whatever the benchmark says.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Attention memory and Ring Attention
question: With Ring Attention on N hosts, after how many compute steps has host 0's query block seen every KV block of the sequence (one layer, forward pass)?
options: N
log2 N
N squared
explain: Each step delivers one new KV block from the predecessor. Host 0 starts with its own block and needs N - 1 more hops, so N compute steps in total (Algorithm 1 loops over the N - 1 transfers).

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
question: A position's halting unit outputs 0.3, 0.5, 0.4 at steps 1 to 3, with epsilon = 0.01. When does it halt and what is its remainder?
options: Step 2, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.2
Step 3, remainder 0.4
It never halts because the sum never equals exactly 0.99
explain: Running sums are 0.3, 0.8, 1.2. The first to reach 0.99 is step 3, so N = 3. The remainder is 1 minus the sum before the halting step: 1 - 0.8 = 0.2. The step-3 halting probability (0.4) is replaced by the remainder so the weights sum to 1.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Exact unlearning: retraining without the data, made cheaper with SISA
question: A SISA system with S = 20 shards batches 60 uniformly random deletion requests before retraining. Roughly what fraction of the shard models must be retrained?
options: About 95%, almost every shard is hit at least once
About 5%, one shard per batch
About 33%, since 60 / 20 = 3 requests per shard on average
100% exactly, because 60 is larger than 20
explain: Each shard escapes all 60 requests with probability (1 - 1/20)^60, about 0.046, so about 95.4% of shards are hit at least once. It is not exactly 100% because some shards can get zero requests by chance. This saturation is why SISA's measured speed-ups shrink as requests pile up.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
question: A lab applies RMU to an open-weight model and publishes near-chance WMDP scores as evidence the model is safe to release. What is the strongest objection?
options: WMDP has too few questions to be meaningful
RMU always destroys general capabilities
With open weights anyone can fine-tune on related data, and RMU did not prevent relearning in the WMDP paper's own fine-tuning experiment
Near-chance scores prove the model was never trained on the data
explain: The WMDP appendix reports that fine-tuning an RMU-unlearned Mistral-7B on the forget corpus recovered performance, and Hu et al. show even benign related data can jog the knowledge back. RMU's stated threat model is a closed model unlearned just before serving, not a public release.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Why one GPU cannot train a 175B model, and the five ways to split it
question: A team has a 1.3B model (about 23 GB of model state at 18 bytes per parameter) that fits on one 80 GB GPU with its activations, and wants to train faster on 64 GPUs. Following the Megatron guidance, what should they try first?
options: TP=8 so every layer is split as finely as possible
Plain data parallelism (DP=64), adding model parallelism only if memory runs out
PP=64 so each GPU holds one or two layers
CP=64 so each GPU holds a sliver of each sequence
explain: The Megatron Core guide says to start with data parallelism and add TP, then PP, only when the model does not fit. Model parallelism adds communication and makes per-GPU matrix multiplies smaller, so it is a cost you pay for memory, not a free speedup.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Distributed optimizer, MoE folding, overlap and measuring MFU
question: Two runs of the same model on the same GPUs both report 160 TFLOP/s per GPU. Run A uses full recompute, run B uses selective recompute. Which trains faster in tokens per second?
options: Run A, because full recompute frees memory for larger batches
They are the same, the TFLOP/s are equal
Run B, because fewer of its FLOPs are wasted on recomputation, so more go to useful model FLOPs
It cannot be decided without knowing the vocabulary size
explain: Both execute FLOPs at the same rate, but A spends about a quarter of them redoing the forward pass. B's model FLOPs per second, and so its MFU and tokens per second, are higher. This is exactly the HFU vs MFU distinction.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Measuring and fixing fragmentation in production
question: A Redis instance reports mem_fragmentation_ratio 2.1, with used_memory 40 MB and RSS 84 MB. What should you do?
options: Probably nothing: 44 MB of absolute overhead is small and includes code and libraries
Enable activedefrag immediately
Restart the instance to reset fragmentation
Lower dirty_decay_ms to 0
explain: The Redis docs warn that a high ratio with only a few megabytes of difference is not an issue: the ratio also counts code, shared libraries and stacks, which dominate a small instance. Check allocator_frag_bytes before acting.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: SeqCst, fences, and when you need one global order
question: Why does `Arc::drop` use Release on every `fetch_sub`, rather than only on the one that reaches zero?
options: Because Release makes the decrement faster on x86
Because no thread knows in advance whether its decrement is the last, and every non-final owner's uses must happen-before the deletion
Because fetch_sub cannot be Relaxed
Because SeqCst is required for reference counts
explain: Whichever thread frees the data needs a happens-before edge from every other owner's last use. Each non-final owner provides that by releasing on its decrement; the final owner acquires (via the fence) before deleting. The Acquire is only needed by the one thread that sees old == 1.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers: announce exactly what you are reading
question: N = 8 threads, K = 2 hazard pointers each, R = 2H. What is the maximum number of retired-but-unfreed nodes, and the minimum freed per scan?
options: 16 and 8
32 and 16
128 and 8
explain: H = N x K = 16, so R = 32. The bound is N x R = 8 x 32 = 256 waiting nodes. Each scan checks 32 nodes and at most 16 can be protected, so it frees at least R minus H = 16.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier
question: A model trained on the Market-1501 training identities reaches high accuracy on held-out images of those same people. Why does that not tell you it will work for re-ID on Market-1501's test split?
options: Because the test images are smaller than training images
Because accuracy is not defined for embeddings
Because the test identities are different people, so what matters is whether distances generalize to unseen identities
Because re-ID only uses the gallery, never the query
explain: Re-ID test identities are disjoint from training identities. Closed-set accuracy on known people says little about whether the embedding separates new people. You need a retrieval evaluation on unseen identities.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking
question: Your team wants to add k-reciprocal re-ranking to a live system that searches a gallery growing by millions of crops per day. What is the main concern?
options: It needs labeled data to retrain the model
It needs neighbor lists for gallery images too, so its cost grows with the gallery and must be recomputed as it changes
It only improves rank-1, never mAP
It only works with ArcFace features
explain: Re-ranking is unsupervised and needs no retraining, but it computes reciprocal neighbors from the gallery's own top-k lists. That is affordable on a fixed benchmark gallery and costly on a large, changing one.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Measurement bias: layout, link order and JIT profiles
question: In a JMH run with forks set to 0, benchmark C is 30% slower when it runs after benchmark D than when it runs alone. What is the right fix?
options: Run each benchmark in its own forked JVM, as JMH does by default
Increase warm-up iterations so the JIT settles
Disable ASLR
Add a Blackhole to benchmark C
explain: C inherits JIT profiles from D in a shared JVM, the effect JMHSample_12_Forking demonstrates. More warm-up in the same JVM keeps the polluted profile. ASLR and Blackholes address layout noise and dead code, which are not the problem here.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: MoE routing replay and low-precision RL
question: You serve a MoE with NVFP4 on B200s to speed up rollout but keep the trainer in BF16 to save engineering time. What do the Miles docs say?
options: Supported; add R3 to cover the drift
Supported only with --use-tis
Supported only on Hopper
Unsupported: NVFP4 rollout needs an NVFP4 trainer forward
explain: The compatibility table allows BF16 training with BF16, FP8 block-wise or MXFP8 rollout, but NVFP4 rollout pairs only with NVFP4 training. The report explains that NVFP4 requires every stage that touches the weights to quantize them.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: LRB: learning to evict like a relaxed Belady
question: LRB samples training examples uniformly over objects in the memory window rather than over requests. Why?
options: Sampling requests would be too slow to compute
Sampling requests over-represents popular objects, while the decisions LRB must learn are mostly about rarely requested objects it should evict
GBMs cannot train on duplicate objects
Objects that are never requested again would be sampled too often
explain: Per-request sampling picks a hot object once per request, so the dataset fills with objects that should obviously stay. The good evictions, objects beyond the boundary including those never requested again, would be rare. The paper samples over objects so both kinds are represented.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Low-rank joint compression: cache one latent, rebuild every head
question: In DeepSeek-V3, which tensors does an MLA layer write to the KV cache for each new token?
options: The per-head keys $k^C$ and values $v^C$
The query latent $c^Q$ and the key latent $c^{KV}$
The layer input $h_t$, since everything can be recomputed from it
The key-value latent $c^{KV}$ and the shared RoPE key $k^R$
explain: Only $c^{KV}$ (512) and $k^R$ (64) are cached. Queries are never cached. Caching $h_t$ (7168 wide) would be larger and would force recomputing projections for every past token.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
question: A blog says MLA alone cut DeepSeek-V2's KV cache by 93.3% vs MHA. What is wrong with that claim?
options: 93.3% is measured against DeepSeek 67B (a GQA model) for the deployed system, which also quantizes the cache; MLA vs MHA in matched models was 14% to 4% of the MHA cache
Nothing, that is exactly what the paper measured
MLA increases the KV cache
93.3% refers to training cost
explain: The abstract compares V2 to DeepSeek 67B. The matched MHA vs MLA comparison is Table 9: 15.6K vs 110.6K and 34.6K vs 860.2K elements per token.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
question: Users ask: "Which of our two vendors had more outages last quarter, and what did each change afterwards?" Retrieval misses half the evidence. What is the best fit?
options: Decompose into sub-questions (outages per vendor, changes per vendor) and retrieve for each
Multi-query with 6 paraphrases and RRF
Raise the RRF constant k
Use the unique union instead of RRF
explain: The question has several distinct parts. Paraphrases of the whole question keep mixing them; sub-questions target each needed fact, in the spirit of SubQuestionQueryEngine or Self-Ask.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Latency budgets and phased ranking in real engines
question: With t1 = 20 ms, k2 = 30 at 960 docs/s and the cheap reranker at 4100 docs/s, what is the largest k1 that fits a 150 ms budget in this model?
options: About 200
About 1000
About 125
About 400
explain: The precise stage costs 1000 x 30 / 960 = 31.25 ms. That leaves 150 - 20 - 31.25 = 98.75 ms for the cheap stage, which scores 4.1 docs per ms: 98.75 x 4.1 = 404.9 candidates.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Shared trunk, n heads, and the memory trick that keeps it cheap
question: In the paper's comparisons, a 4-token model and its next-token baseline have equal parameter counts. How?
options: The 4-token model uses a smaller vocabulary
The heads are linear layers with no parameters worth counting
Three layers are removed from the trunk to pay for the three extra head layers
The baseline is trained on four times fewer tokens
explain: Each head is one transformer layer. Adding n - 1 extra head layers and removing n - 1 trunk layers keeps the total equal, so gains cannot be explained by extra parameters.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Shampoo: one preconditioner for the rows, one for the columns
question: A layer has weight shape $16384 \times 4096$. Which part of Shampoo's state dominates memory and root-computation cost?
options: The right factor R, because it multiplies the inputs
The momentum buffer, because it is the same size as the weight
Both factors equally, since Shampoo is symmetric
The left factor L: it is 16384 x 16384 (268M entries) and its eigendecomposition costs on the order of 16384^3
explain: $L$ is $m \times m$ with $m = 16384$, so it has $2.7 \times 10^8$ entries versus $1.7 \times 10^7$ for $R$, and eigendecomposition scales as the cube of the side. This is why implementations block large dimensions, and why SOAP and its variants sometimes skip the larger side.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs, distributing it, and choosing an optimizer
question: With ZeRO-1, why does Distributed Muon need an extra collective that distributed AdamW does not?
options: Newton-Schulz needs the full momentum matrix, but each rank only holds a shard of it
Muon's momentum is stored in fp64 and must be broadcast
Muon recomputes gradients on every rank
Muon needs the Hessian, which is sharded across ranks
explain: AdamW's update is elementwise, so a rank can update its shard alone. Orthogonalization mixes all entries of the matrix, so Moonlight adds a bf16 DP gather of the momentum, runs Newton-Schulz on the full matrix and keeps only the local slice.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: Verifying a muP implementation, and where muP stops
question: A coord check of your muP Transformer shows the attention logits growing roughly like the square root of width after two steps, while every other curve is flat. What is the most likely bug?
options: Attention still divides q.k by sqrt(d_head) instead of d_head
The base width is too small
Weight decay is not scaled
The learning rate is too small for a coord check
explain: Once q and k become correlated during training, $q^\top k$ grows like $d$, so a $1/\sqrt{d}$ scale leaves logits growing like $\sqrt{d}$ times their target size as heads widen, while the rest of the network is fine. Switching to $1/d$ (or 8/d as in the README) fixes it.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Building a mutex on a futex: the three-state lock
question: A thread calls lock on an unlocked three-state mutex and later unlocks it, with no other thread involved. How many system calls happen?
options: One: the wake in unlock
Two: a wait and a wake
One: the CAS is a system call
Zero
explain: The CAS turns 0 into 1 in user space. At unlock the swap returns 1, not 2, so the wake is skipped. Atomic instructions are not system calls; the kernel never sees an uncontended lock.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Write skew: the bug that snapshot isolation lets through
question: Which change makes the doctors example safe while staying at Repeatable Read?
options: Run both transactions with a shorter timeout
Add an index on the on_call column
Lock the rows being counted, for example SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on all on-call doctors, so the second transaction waits and then fails or sees the change
Switch to Read Committed so each statement sees fresh data
explain: Write skew comes from reads that do not conflict with the other transaction's write. Turning the reads into row locks (FOR UPDATE) materializes the conflict: the second transaction blocks, then hits a concurrent update error at Repeatable Read. Read Committed does not help; both counts can still run before either update.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: BIO, IOB1 and BIOES: tag sets that make spans decodable
question: In the CoNLL-2003 data files, when does a B-ORG tag appear?
options: Only when an organisation starts immediately after another organisation ends
At the start of every organisation entity
On every token of a multi-token organisation except the first
Only on single-token organisations
explain: The files use IOB1, the Ramshaw and Marcus scheme: entity tokens are I-ORG by default, and B-ORG marks only the leftmost token of an organisation that immediately follows another organisation. The option saying every organisation entity starts with B-ORG describes IOB2, which is what most modern pipelines convert the files to.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: Few labels, new domain, and the failure modes that remain
question: Your log tagger scores 91 F1 on a weakly labelled held-out split and 62 F1 on 200 hand-labelled lines. What is the most likely cause?
options: The weakly labelled split shares the labelling functions' blind spots, so it rewards reproducing them rather than finding entities
The hand-labelled set is too small for the metric to be meaningful
The model overfitted the 200 hand-labelled lines
Entity F1 is not comparable across splits
explain: A test set built by the same regexes and gazetteers as the training labels cannot reveal what those functions miss. The tagger gets credit for imitating them. Only human labels measure the task, which is why some of your annotation budget must be held out and never used for training.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Hardware alignment: the kernel and the measured speedups
question: Why does NSA's selection kernel loop over GQA groups at each query position, instead of tiling a block of consecutive queries like FlashAttention?
options: Consecutive queries can select different KV blocks, so a query tile would cause scattered, redundant loads, while heads of one group share exactly the same blocks
Triton cannot tile over the query dimension
It reduces the number of compressed tokens
It makes the selection differentiable
explain: Within a group, every head reads the same selected blocks, so each contiguous block load is reused h times. Consecutive positions have no such guarantee, so tiling them would not share loads.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: pHash: hashing the low frequencies of a DCT
question: Your service computes pHash with library X; a partner sends pHashes computed with library Y for the same images. Distances between matching pairs are around 30 of 64. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The partner's images were heavily edited
Hamming distance is undefined across libraries
pHash is random by design
Libraries differ in details such as resize filter, mean versus median and whether DC is included, so their bits are not comparable
explain: pHash is a family of variants. Krawetz uses a mean without DC, ImageHash a median with DC, and resampling filters differ too. Meta's PDQ documentation makes the same point: even one algorithm in different languages can give different hashes, so it defines conformance against the reference implementation.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: The three contracts: policy, generation and environment interfaces
question: You write a custom environment that runs unit tests. It returns `rewards` as a dict `{"tests": ..., "style": ...}`. GDPO training fails to find the components. What is the most likely bug?
options: Environments may only return a single Tensor
The keys must use the reward/ prefix, for example reward/tests
Rewards must be Python lists, not tensors
Multi-reward environments must set terminateds to all zeros
explain: The environments guide states that each key of a multi-reward dict must use the reward/ prefix. The rollout then stores the summed total_reward and each named component for GDPO.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
question: A program's working set fits entirely in each core's L1 and L2 caches. How much does NUMA placement of its data matter during the steady state?
options: A lot: every load must check the home node of the address first
It matters only for writes, since reads are always served locally
Very little: cache hits never leave the core, so the node only matters on misses
explain: Placement only changes the cost of requests that go out to DRAM. Hits in private caches are served inside the core no matter which node owns the page. NUMA effects show up when the working set misses the caches, or when cores on different sockets share written cache lines.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Worked example: what placement costs in latency and bandwidth
question: A latency-bound service (pointer chasing, one outstanding miss at a time) runs one thread per node. Which placement is best for it?
options: Keep each thread's data on its own node
Interleave all memory, to use both controllers
Bind everything to node 0 for predictability
explain: With one outstanding miss at a time, bandwidth is not the limit; every miss pays the latency. Local placement gives f = 0, the lowest average latency. Interleave would make half the misses remote.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Garbage collection and the write amplification formula
question: Two drives have identical flash. Drive X exposes 960 GB from 1024 GB of flash, drive Y exposes 1000 GB. Under sustained random overwrites, which is true?
options: Same write amplification, since the flash is identical
Y has lower write amplification because it has more capacity to spread writes
X has higher amplification because GC runs more often
X has lower write amplification because more spare means emptier victims
explain: X has S_f = 64/1024, about 6.3%; Y has 24/1024, about 2.3%. Less spare means victims are fuller when cleaned, and A = 1/(1-u) rises steeply as u approaches 1.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Removing duplicates: greedy NMS and DETR's set prediction
question: A people-counting deployment in a packed train station uses NMS at IoU 0.5 and consistently undercounts. Which change is most likely to help?
options: Raise the NMS IoU threshold (or use a detector that needs no NMS), because overlapping people are being suppressed as duplicates
Lower the NMS IoU threshold to 0.3
Raise the confidence threshold to remove false positives
Switch to xywh box format
explain: Undercounting in crowds is the signature of NMS deleting true boxes whose IoU with a neighbor exceeds the threshold. Lowering it to 0.3 would suppress even more. A higher threshold, or a set-prediction detector, keeps overlapping people. Raising the confidence threshold removes boxes, so it would lower the count further.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Object storage is a strange kind of disk
question: Which S3 guarantee is what lets a brand-new node read a file that another node wrote a moment ago, without any coordination between the two nodes?
options: Eleven nines of durability
Strong read-after-write consistency for PUTs
Storage across at least 3 Availability Zones
Per-prefix request rate scaling
explain: Durability and multiple AZs keep data safe, but a reader could still see a stale or missing object if S3 were eventually consistent. Strong read-after-write consistency means any GET or LIST that starts after a successful PUT returns the new object, so a fresh node can trust what it reads.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Tiered storage versus S3-native: choosing a design
question: A team enables tiered storage and expects produce latency to drop because brokers now have less data on disk. What actually happens to produce latency?
options: It drops, since disks are less full
It rises to S3 PUT latency
It becomes unpredictable because acks wait for remote copies
It is essentially unchanged: produce still goes through the leader and in-sync replicas; remote copying happens later, for rolled segments only
explain: Tiering changes what happens to data after a segment rolls. The produce path, leader append plus replication to in-sync replicas, is the same as without tiering, so latency does not drop or rise because of it. The wins are smaller disks and faster broker replacement and rebalancing.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Why OCR is a pipeline: find the text, then read it
question: A receipt pipeline reads every character correctly, yet it reports the subtotal as the total. Which stage most likely failed?
options: Layout analysis and field mapping: the right words were read but linked to the wrong field
Text detection: the total was never found
Recognition: the digits were misread
Binarization: the image was too dark
explain: If every character was read correctly, detection and recognition did their jobs. Picking the wrong number is a structure problem, which is exactly what the layout-aware models in lesson 5 address.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: A build is a graph: why one edit rebuilds 4 files, not 1 or 500
question: In the tiny project, you edit ops.h. Which objects recompile?
options: Only add.o and matmul.o, since ops.h declares their functions
add.o, matmul.o and main.o
All 5 objects, because ops.h includes tensor.h
None until you run a clean build
explain: add.cpp, matmul.cpp and main.cpp include ops.h, so 3 of 5 objects recompile. The include edge tensor.h to ops.h points the other way: editing ops.h does not affect files that only include tensor.h, such as tensor.cpp.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CUDA builds: PTX, cubins and the architecture list
question: A CUDA-heavy project takes 90 minutes to build with CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=all. You only need to test on your own CC 8.9 GPU. Which change cuts build time the most while still running locally?
options: Set CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (or 89)
Switch the generator from Ninja to Makefiles
Set CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=MinSizeRel
Use 89-virtual so the driver compiles at startup
explain: With all, every .cu file is compiled for every supported real architecture plus PTX; a single native target removes nearly all of that repeated device compilation. 89-virtual also builds once, but then every run JIT compiles all kernels at startup, which is slow for a large project.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Why flaky tests ruin big suites: the probability
question: A maintainer proposes `--reruns 3` globally to fix red CI. Which concern is most serious?
options: Reruns make pytest exit with code 5
A real race condition that fails 50 percent of runs would be reported only $0.5^4 = 6.25$ percent of the time
Reruns are not supported on GitHub Actions
Reruns change the order tests are collected in
explain: With 3 reruns a test is reported failed only if all 4 attempts fail. For a real intermittent bug with $q = 0.5$, that is $0.5^4 = 0.0625$, so about 94 percent of runs would be green despite the bug.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Giving review: reading order and comments that land
question: Which comment is phrased the way this lesson recommends?
options: "You clearly didn't test this."
"Nit: this could be a list comprehension, but the loop is fine too."
"This is wrong."
"Why would anyone write it like this?"
explain: It is labeled (Nit: tells the author it is optional), it is about the code, and it says the existing version is acceptable. The others aim at the person or give no reason and no way forward.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: Codes of conduct: scope, reporting and the enforcement ladder
question: You find a way to read other users' files through a project's upload endpoint. The repo has SECURITY.md and private vulnerability reporting enabled. What do you do?
options: Use the private report (or the channel SECURITY.md names) and follow its instructions
Open a detailed public issue so the fix gets attention quickly
Open a PR with the fix and describe the exploit in the PR body
Post a minimal reproducer in the project's public chat
explain: Public issues, PRs and chat disclose the vulnerability before a fix ships. SECURITY.md gives the project's reporting instructions, and private vulnerability reporting delivers the report only to maintainers.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Keeping a branch current: rebase onto upstream/main
question: Halfway through a rebase, Git stops with a conflict in `parser.c` and you are unsure of your fix. Which command returns the branch to exactly where it was before you started?
options: `git rebase --skip`
`git rebase --abort`
`git rebase --continue`
`git reset --hard upstream/main`
explain: `--abort` stops the rebase and restores the original branch. `--skip` drops the conflicting commit and keeps going, which loses that change. `--continue` needs the conflict resolved and staged. Resetting to upstream/main throws away all your commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: No license means no permission: what a license grants
question: Your company uses an Apache-2.0 library and later files a patent suit claiming that library infringes one of its patents. What happens under section 3?
options: The patent licenses your company received for that library terminate as of the filing date
The copyright license terminates and you must stop using the code
Nothing, because Apache-2.0 only covers copyright
The library's contributors lose their own patents
explain: Section 3 grants a patent license from each contributor, and it terminates for anyone who starts patent litigation alleging the Work infringes. The copyright license in section 2 is not what terminates.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: The DCO: certifying every commit with Signed-off-by
question: A project wants contributor provenance with minimal friction for drive-by contributors, and does not need any rights beyond its license. Which fits best?
options: A corporate CLA with each contributor's employer
The DCO with a sign-off check on every commit
An individual CLA signed before any PR is reviewed
No policy, since inbound=outbound needs no record at all
explain: The DCO adds one trailer per commit and no paperwork, while still recording a certification of origin. CLAs suit projects that want an explicit, signed grant (often including patents); no policy leaves no record of who certified the code's origin.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Map the repository before you read a line of it
question: Your search for a function name returns 40 hits, 30 of them under deps/. What is the best next step for a Redis server bug?
options: Read all 40 hits in order
Delete deps/ from your clone so search is faster
Search only the tests
Restrict the search to src, for example `git grep -n name -- src`, since deps is vendored third-party code
explain: Vendored code is a copy of another project. Bugs there are usually fixed upstream, not in this repo. A pathspec after `--` limits git grep to the directories that matter without changing the checkout.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
question: A maintainer replies "works for me" to your report. Which addition is most likely to turn it into a reproduction?
options: A longer description of how important the bug is to your team
The exact versions of the library, Python and OS you ran, plus the input that triggered it as text
A screenshot of the stack trace with the failing line circled
A link to your full private application repository
explain: "Works for me" usually means your environment or input differs from theirs in a way the report did not capture. Exact versions and the triggering input close that gap. A screenshot is not searchable, a private repo is not runnable by them, and urgency does not help them see the bug.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
question: Your repro fails on your GPU machine but passes on the maintainer's CPU-only laptop, even with `torch.manual_seed(0)`. What is the most useful next step?
options: Assume the maintainer made a mistake and ask them to retry
Remove the seed, since it obviously does not help
Report the device and the collect_env output, and check whether the failure needs the GPU path (for example, run your repro on CPU yourself)
explain: PyTorch's notes say results can differ between CPU and GPU even with identical seeds. Checking whether the failure needs the GPU narrows the hidden variable, and the environment report lets the maintainer match your setup.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Why contiguous KV allocation wastes most of the memory
question: A request reserves 2048 contiguous slots and finishes after 300 tokens. What kind of waste are the 1748 untouched slots?
options: External fragmentation, because they sit between other requests
Internal fragmentation, because they are inside the request's own chunk and were never used
Reserved slots, because they will be used by later tokens of the same request
No waste, because the allocator frees them when the request ends
explain: They are inside the request's allocation and were never filled, which is internal fragmentation. The paper notes it is only known to be waste after the request finishes. Reserved slots are the ones that will eventually be filled; external fragmentation is space between allocations.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Why profilers sample stacks instead of timing every call
question: You profile with `perf record -F 99 -a -g -- sleep 10` on an 8-CPU machine where every CPU is busy. Roughly how many samples do you get?
explain: -F is per CPU and -a samples all CPUs: 99 x 10 s x 8 CPUs = 7920. 990 would be one CPU. 320,000 is what perf's 4000 Hz default would give on all 8 CPUs.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: A profiling workflow, its costs and its blind spots
question: You run `perf record -g ./server` as a normal user on a stock kernel and the flame graph has no kernel frames at all. Most likely reason?
options: perf_event_paranoid defaults to 2, which blocks kernel profiling without CAP_PERFMON
The server never makes system calls
-g only records kernel stacks when -F is given
Kernel frames are filtered by stackcollapse-perf.pl
explain: At paranoid level 2 an unprivileged user may profile their own user-space code but not the kernel. Run with CAP_PERFMON or root, or lower the sysctl on a machine you control.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Transactions: how libpmemobj's undo log survives a crash
question: In an undo-log transaction, which ordering is required for correctness?
options: Modify the data in place, then write the undo entry, then fence
Make the undo entry durable, then modify the data in place
Invalidate the log, then flush the modified data
Flush the data only after the log has been invalidated, to save a fence
explain: Recovery can only roll back what the log holds. If the data change could become durable first, a crash leaves new data with no old copy. Invalidating the log is the commit point, so it must come after the data is durable.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Shrinking a struct by reordering its fields
question: Which change can never shrink a C struct?
options: Moving the char fields to the end
Reordering fields so larger alignments come first
Moving a pointer field from the end to the front of a struct whose other fields are all pointers
Replacing an int field with a short when the values fit
explain: If every field is a pointer, every offset is already a multiple of 8 and there is no padding to remove, so moving one pointer changes nothing. The other options can each remove padding or bytes.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Backbones, top-down versus bottom-up, and part affinity fields
question: Which change would most directly break the PAF score for a correct elbow-wrist pair?
options: Another person stands far away in the frame
The predicted field along the segment points sideways, across the forearm, instead of along it
The elbow heatmap peak is 0.6 instead of 0.9
The PAF predicts the wrist-to-elbow direction, and scoring uses the same convention
explain: The score is the dot product between the field and the segment direction. If the field along the segment points sideways, the dot products shrink. Distant people do not touch this segment, the peak height does not enter E, and a consistent direction convention is fine.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Pre-filtering: allow lists and brute force over the matches
question: Which query is the best fit for pre-filtering followed by a flat scan?
options: 50 million vectors, filter language = en matching 60% of them
2 million vectors, filter user_id = 42 matching 800 vectors
2 million vectors, no filter at all
50 million vectors, filter year > 2000 matching 90% of them
explain: Brute force costs one distance per matching vector. 800 distances is trivial and exact. The other cases would scan millions of vectors, where a graph search touches only a small fraction.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Little's law: how many misses must be in flight
question: A core keeps 16 lines in flight and memory latency rises from 80 ns to 120 ns. Peak DRAM bandwidth is not the limit. What happens to this core's bandwidth?
options: It stays at 12.8 GB/s because peak bandwidth did not change
It drops to about 8.5 GB/s
It rises, because longer latency means more lines are in flight
It drops to 0.8 GB/s
explain: With concurrency capped at 16 lines, $B = 16 \times 64 / 120 \approx 8.53$ GB/s. Little's law says bandwidth is concurrency divided by latency, so longer latency at fixed concurrency means less bandwidth.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
question: A generator samples 100 solutions to a hard olympiad problem; 97 have wrong final answers. Why is outcome supervision on this problem a weak training signal for a reward model?
options: Outcome labels are noisy because the answer checker is usually wrong
Almost every label is 0, and a 0 does not say which step failed, so the model learns little about where reasoning breaks
Outcome labels cannot be computed for olympiad problems
The reward model would overfit to the 3 correct solutions and ignore the rest
explain: When nearly all solutions are wrong, a 0 is the expected label and says only 'some step was wrong'. Lightman et al. make exactly this credit-assignment argument: process labels also say how many leading steps were right and where the first mistake is.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Failure modes, evaluation, and why some labs skip PRMs
question: Which of these was NOT one of DeepSeek-R1's stated reasons for not using a PRM in large-scale RL?
options: Defining a fine-grained step in general reasoning is hard
Judging intermediate-step correctness is hard, and manual labels do not scale
A model-based PRM leads to reward hacking and retraining adds overhead
PRMs cannot rerank top-N responses or assist guided search
explain: DeepSeek-R1 says the opposite: PRMs show good ability to rerank top-N responses and assist guided search. Their objection was that the benefit in large-scale RL did not outweigh the extra compute and complexity.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a switch really costs: direct work and cold caches
question: Why is switching between two threads of the same process usually cheaper than between two processes, even though both save and restore the same registers?
options: Threads have fewer registers
The address space stays loaded, so there is no page table switch, no TLB flush and the shared code and data may still be in cache
The kernel does not run the scheduler for threads
Thread switches happen entirely in user space on Linux
explain: With NPTL's 1:1 model the kernel schedules threads like any task, so the scheduler and register work are the same. The saving is the address space: no CR3 write, valid TLB entries, and shared data that may still be warm.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: IVFADC: inverted lists with residual codes
question: An IVFPQ index with nlist = 1024 and PQ64 has poor recall. Profiling shows the true nearest neighbor is usually in the 3rd or 4th nearest list. Which change helps most?
options: Switch to PQ128 codes
Reduce nlist to 64 so lists are bigger
Turn off residual encoding
Increase nprobe from 1 to 8
explain: Neighbors in unprobed lists are never scored, so better codes cannot find them. Raising nprobe scans those lists. Shrinking nlist also captures them but scans a much larger fraction per probe; the paper finds that for a fixed fraction visited, more lists with more probes is more accurate.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Noising frames: Gaussians on positions, IGSO(3) on orientations
question: Why does the rotation part of the forward process use IGSO(3) instead of adding Gaussian noise to the nine entries of R?
options: IGSO(3) is faster to sample than a Gaussian
Because a Gaussian perturbation of the nine entries leaves a matrix that is not orthonormal, so it is not a rotation at all
Because rotations have nine degrees of freedom and Gaussians only model three
Because the loss must be invariant to global rotation
explain: SO(3) is a curved manifold embedded in 9-dimensional space. Adding independent Gaussian noise to the entries leaves the manifold: columns stop being orthonormal and the determinant stops being 1. IGSO(3) is the transition density of Brownian motion that stays on the manifold.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym expansion on the toy corpus: recall up, precision at risk
question: In the toy corpus, why did vehicle contribute 0.896 to d3 while car contributed only 0.666 to d1, both in 4-token documents?
options: vehicle appears in 1 document and car in 2, so vehicle has the higher IDF
Synonyms get an automatic 1.35x boost
d3 is shorter than d1
car is a stop word in this analyzer
explain: Same length and term frequency, so the difference is IDF: 1.992 for df 1 against 1.482 for df 2. Lucene's SynonymQuery avoids this by using the maximum df of the group.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Why the query the user typed is rarely the query to send
question: Which transformation is decomposition rather than rewriting or expansion?
options: Turning `how does it fail` into `how does Raft handle leader failure`
Appending `automobile` to a query that says `car`
Turning `compare Raft and Paxos leader election` into one query about Raft and one about Paxos
Correcting `recieve` to `receive`
explain: Decomposition produces several sub-queries that are retrieved separately. Resolving it to Raft and fixing a typo are rewrites (one query in, one query out); appending a synonym is expansion.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Interleave, step back, or fan out: IRCoT, Step-Back and multi-query
question: What is the key difference between IRCoT and Self-Ask?
options: IRCoT trains the retriever; Self-Ask does not
IRCoT uses each generated reasoning sentence as the next retrieval query, while Self-Ask writes explicit follow-up questions and inserts search answers
Self-Ask retrieves once; IRCoT retrieves once per document
They are the same algorithm with different names
explain: Both interleave retrieval with generation and both are prompting-only. Self-Ask sends explicit sub-questions to search and pastes back short answers; IRCoT sends its chain-of-thought sentences to a paragraph retriever and accumulates up to 15 paragraphs for a final reader.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error
question: RaBitQ errors at D = 256 are too large for you. Following the 1/sqrt(D) rule, how many code bits per vector would halve the error?
explain: Error scales as 1/sqrt(D), so halving it needs 4x the bits: 1024. The paper notes you can lengthen codes by padding vectors with zeros before rotation; padded dimensions are not kept in the raw vectors.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Paxos: choosing one value with prepare and accept
question: A proposer finished phase 1 with number 7. Promises: A1 accepted (2, X), A2 accepted (4, Y), A3 accepted nothing. Which value must it send in accept(7, ?)
options: X, because it was accepted first
Its own value, because no value had a majority
Either X or Y, whichever it prefers
Y, the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal
explain: The rule picks the value of the highest-numbered proposal among the replies, here (4, Y). Y might already be chosen through a majority this proposer did not contact; (2, X) was never chosen: if it had been, every higher-numbered proposal issued, including (4, Y), would carry X.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Consensus in production: reads, membership, timeouts
question: With Pre-Vote enabled, a server returns after 10 minutes in a network partition. What happens to the current leader?
options: It steps down because the returning server has a much higher term
It must run a new election to admit the server
Nothing: the server never raised its term while isolated, and returns to follower when the leader's heartbeat reaches it
It is removed from the cluster configuration
explain: While partitioned, the server could not get pre-votes from a majority, so it never incremented its term. On reconnecting, the other servers are still hearing heartbeats and refuse its pre-vote; once the leader's heartbeat reaches it, it settles as a follower in the same term.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Prompting the generator to answer with citations
question: Which prompt change most directly reduces confident answers to questions the corpus cannot answer?
options: Raising the sampling temperature
Moving the question before the sources
Asking for longer answers
Instructing the model to say it does not know when the sources lack the answer
explain: Barnett et al.'s first failure point is a question the documents cannot answer, where the system should say it does not know but can be fooled into answering. An explicit abstain instruction is the first defense; checking it needs test questions whose answer is absent.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Query-document features: BM25 per field, coverage, proximity
question: Document X has the query terms in its body at positions 4, 5 and 6. Document Y has them at positions 2, 40 and 77. Their body BM25 scores are equal. Which feature tells them apart?
options: Body BM25 with a larger k1
Body coverage ratio
Body length
Minimum window (proximity)
explain: Both contain all terms, so coverage is 1.0 for both, and BM25 ignores positions entirely. Only a positional feature such as the minimum covering window (3 versus 76) separates them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Feature logging: train on exactly the numbers you serve
question: Offline NDCG of the new model is excellent, but online it underperforms the old one. Features were computed by a Python script for training and by the search engine for serving. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether the learning rate was too high
Whether NDCG is the right metric
Whether the model has too few trees
Whether the two pipelines produce identical feature values for the same query-document pairs
explain: Train/serve skew is the prime suspect when offline and online disagree. Log the engine's feature vectors for a sample of pairs and diff them against the script's values. Fixing the model cannot help if its inputs differ.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Implementation gotchas: ties, ideals, missing queries
question: A colleague's evaluation writes every result with score 0.0 and the correct rank in the rank column, then runs trec_eval. What happens?
options: All documents tie on score, so trec_eval orders them by docno string, scrambling the ranking
trec_eval uses the rank column, so results are correct
trec_eval rejects the file
trec_eval reports every metric as 0
explain: trec_eval sorts by the score column and breaks ties by docno (reverse string order); it never reads the rank column. With all scores equal, the ranking becomes an ordering of document IDs, and every rank-sensitive metric is measured on that order instead.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
